schools.summary: Henry reads the invitation as pious, not political — 'not to bring them back to the house of David, but to the Lord God of Israel'; a prince rendering good for evil.
Clarke explains Hoshea's tolerance and that the calves had already been carried off by Assyria; Wesley reads 'Israel' of the ten-tribe remnant, named by its two chief tribes as nearest.
Ellicott notes 'letters' (iggeroth) a late Persian loanword and dates Hezekiah's first year to Hoshea's third (2 Kings 17:2).
Gill: the king sent to his own subjects and to the northern Israelites dwelling in Judah alike.

outliers.note: Distinctively grounds the free proclamation in the claim that the golden calves had already been carried off — Dan by Tiglath-pileser, Bethel by Shalmaneser.

schools.summary: Keil glosses lemaddai ('to sufficiency') of the priesthood in general, not mere numbers, grounding the second-month keeping in Numbers 9:6, 11; Ellicott sets the council's resolve before 14 Nisan.
Clarke and Wesley: the temple's purgation could not be finished till the 16th, so the feast must be held late or lost a year; the individual proviso (Num. 9:10) was extended to the congregation.
Gill: the king, nobles, and national senate took counsel together.

Ellicott fixes the reopening (29:17) and the rare lemaddai ('unto what was enough') meaning too few priests purified in time; Keil weighs 'not in multitude' and doubts Rashi's temporal reading of larob.
Gill: they could not keep it in Nisan because the temple's cleansing was unfinished till the 16th.
Wesley reads 'sufficiently' of both manner and number, too few priests for so many paschal victims (cf. 29:34).

themes: a nation estranged from its worship

schools.summary: Ellicott specifies what was approved — the second-month keeping and the northern invitation; Keil traces the decree formally established and proclaimed on the nation's shared judgment, warranted by Numbers 9.
Gill: they all unanimously agreed, and determined it should be done.

Ellicott renders 'decreed a proposal' and 'not in multitude had they kept it' (Jerusalem the only lawful place, cf. 2 Kings 23:22); Keil rejects Rashi's temporal reading of larob for the numerical sense.
Gill: they passed a vote appointing heralds, that none might plead ignorance.

debates.question: Does 'they had not done it of a long time' render larob temporally or numerically?

sides.position: 'not in multitude' — the people had not come in their numbers
'not for a long time' — the neglect dated from the schism
holders: Rashi (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

schools.summary: Keil: the runners added spoken exhortation to the written invitation; Ellicott presses 'remnant' (peletah, survivors) as a backward glance to Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser's inroads (2 Kings 18:9), the couriers likely body-guardsmen.
Henry reads the summons as a preacher's logic of repentance — children of Israel bound to the God of Abraham, a remnant that must shelter under him lest they be swallowed up.
Clarke fixes 'posts' (ratsim) as the trusted, swift-footed royal couriers.
Gill: the posts went through both kingdoms, north and south alike.
Ellicott dates the fathers' apostasy from Jeroboam and identifies the captive brethren of Naphtali and trans-Jordan; both render 'desolation' as 'an astonishment' (cf. 29:8).
Henry: 'let their harms be your warnings' — the wreck of the ten tribes is the sermon God preached to the survivors, the most terrible of the letter's arguments.
Gill reads the trespass as calf-worship and neglect of the temple, citing the Targum's 'acted deceitfully with the Word.'

themes: let their harms be your warnings

schools.summary: Keil reads 'give the hand' as a covenant pledge of fidelity (2 Kings 10:15; Ezra 10:19); Ellicott renders 'yield a hand to Jehovah,' sets 'harden not your neck' beside 2 Kings 17:14, and notes the language betrays an ideal cast.
Henry unfolds the given hand as covenant consent — 'give him your hand in token of giving him your heart' (Isa. 44:5) — the iron sinew of the neck bowed to God's yoke.
Gill glosses 'stiffnecked' as obstinate, like a heifer unused to the yoke.

themes: give the hand to the LORD

schools.summary: Keil spells out the conditional promise — exiles pitied by their captors and restored — grounded in Exodus 34:6; Ellicott fixes rahamim as the compassion a captor is made to feel (Ps. 106:46; Neh. 9:17).
Clarke gives the Targum's pledge — God 'will not cause his majesty to ascend up' — the abiding shechinah, the Divine Presence that will not withdraw from a returning people.
Henry's maxim: 'if you return to God in a way of duty, he will return to you in a way of mercy,' with hope of the captivity turned again.
Gill reads 'turn again' of turning to the fear and worship of the Lord.

themes: if ye return he will return

schools.summary: Keil defends 'from city to city' — the Assyrians spared many villages; Ellicott marks Zebulun as the couriers' limit (not Dan), an incidental note lending historical truth (Isa. 9:1), the verb picturing continual scorn.
Henry: they refused with disdain, and their contempt — with ruin two or three years off — hastened and aggravated it, leaving them inexcusable.
Wesley: the generality had lost their appetite for God's ordinances, and about six years later were carried captive (2 Kings 18:10).
Gill: Hoshea, a better king, did not hinder his people from worshipping at Jerusalem.

themes: grace turned to a savour of death

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the responding tribes (with Ephraim and Issachar of v.18) are self-consistent given the couriers' reach, and 'humbled themselves' means repented (12:6); Keil lets the plain fact stand.
Henry: 'in the worst of times God has had a remnant'; the difference was humility — 'pride keeps men from yielding; when that is brought down, the work is done.'
Gill reads the humbling as real repentance — confession of idolatry, sorrow, willingness to obey.
Ellicott and Keil note 'the hand of God,' usually punitive (Exod. 9:3), is here a helping hand for good (Ezra 8:22), the royal command itself inspired 'by the word of the LORD' (cf. 29:15).
Henry: 'the hand of God gave them that one heart; it is in the day of power that Christ's subjects are made willing' — God works both to will and to do.
Wesley: God by his grace inclined hearts lately given to idolatry to unanimous compliance — the reason of the wonderful change.
Gill traces the hearty unanimity to the power and efficacy of divine grace.

themes: the hand of God for good

schools.summary: Keil marks the swelling into a great congregation; Ellicott fixes larob me'od ('in great multitude'), the answer to the fifth verse's lament that the feast had not been kept in multitude.
Henry reads the great, lively gathering as the first fruit of the reformation — a people famished of God's ordinances crowding to keep them.
Gill: they came out of the several tribes, north and south together.

Keil: they removed Ahaz's illegal altars (28:24) and cast them into the Kidron (29:16); Ellicott notes Ahaz's altars 'in every corner' and the rare word for the incense-burners — the city purified as the temple was.
Henry: 'before they kept the feast, they cast out this old leaven' — the best preparation for the gospel passover is to cast away our spiritual idolatries.
Gill fixes the timing — they did this before they slew and ate the Passover.

Keil reads the shame as driving priests and Levites to sanctify themselves (the country clergy, not the Jerusalem Levites praised in 29:34); Ellicott specifies shame at former reluctance and calls the Levites' inclusion a small verbal inaccuracy for brevity.
Henry: the people so forward that priests and Levites blushed to be outdone by the commonalty, which put them on a wholesome, sanctifying shame.
Wesley: the people's forwardness upbraided the clergy's remissness — 'the zeal of others should make us ashamed of our own coldness.'
Gill: though not in the proper month, they kept it on the proper day, the fourteenth.

themes: shame as a means of grace

schools.summary: Keil explains the priests sprinkled the blood from the Levites' hand — not the ordinary rule, since normally the offerer handed it up — because many were unclean; Ellicott glosses omdam and 'after their manner.'
Henry lifts the sprinkled blood to 'a type of Christ our passover sacrificed for us' (1 Cor. 5:7) — the applying of the blood the heart of the rite.
Gill: priests and Levites each stood in their appointed place for the sacrifice.

themes: a type of Christ our Passover

schools.summary: Keil: the Levites slew for the unclean to sanctify the lambs, since a lamb slain by unclean hands would be defiled; Ellicott notes the expedient recurs unapologized at 35:6, the precedent become rule (cf. Ezra 6:20).
Henry marks it a pardonable irregularity — the Levites killed the lambs that each man should have killed, assisting beyond the law's ordinary allowance.
Gill: many were unpurified from uncleanness by idolatry or ceremonial defilement, with no time to cleanse themselves.

Ellicott: the four tribes betray a documentary source; they ate illegally, unclean (Num. 9:6), condoned because Hezekiah prayed; 'pardon' is 'make atonement for' (Lev. 16:6). Keil corrects the verse-division, joining the intercession to v.19.
Henry: the priests were loth to turn away new converts, and (with Grotius) ritual institutions must give way to public benefit, not necessity only.
Clarke reckons them excusable, from wholly idolatrous countries, and renders the Targum's prayer, 'have mercy on this people who err.'
Gill traces the uncleanness to the ten tribes, where idolatry had long prevailed.

Ellicott renders 'hath directed his heart,' corrects the verse-division (cf. 1 Chron. 15:12), marks the prayer's preference of spiritual sincerity over literal observance, and notes 'purification of the sanctuary' found only here; Keil joins the clause to the king's atoning cry.
Henry: where the heart is sincere there may be defects short of the sanctuary's purity, real sins of omission needing pardoning grace through the blood of Christ.
Wesley distinguishes the outward 'purification of the sanctuary' from the inward purity acknowledged here — the great thing is to prepare the heart to seek God.
Gill reads it of the worshipper desirous of God's worship, noting Aben Ezra referred it to Hezekiah.

debates.question: Whose is the heart that 'prepareth to seek God' — the worshipper's or Hezekiah's?

schools.summary: Keil takes 'healed' of the soul from sin (Hosea 14:4; Jer. 3:22); Ellicott of a plague averted, the wrath threatened against uncleanness (Lev. 15:31), comparing Abimelech's healing (Gen. 20:17).
Henry: healing denotes not only forgiveness (Ps. 103:3) but comfort and peace (Isa. 57:18); the Lord was well pleased with the king's concern.
Wesley reads 'healed' simply as pardoned — accepted them and their services as if clean.
Gill: God heard, accepted, and granted what the king desired.

debates.question: What does it mean that God 'healed the people'?

sides.position: healing of the soul from sin regarded as a spiritual disease
the staying of a literal plague uncleanness had deserved
simply the pardon and acceptance of their worship

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott read 'instruments of strength to Jehovah' — with which the singers ascribed power to God (Ps. 29:1) — Ellicott granting the AV's 'loud instruments' has warrant in the chronicler's love of strong music (5:13).
Henry: they praised day by day with song and instrument — 'praising God should be much of our work in our religious assemblies,' not the ornament of worship but a chief part of its work.
Gill: the seven days of unleavened bread always followed the Passover by the law of Moses.

debates.question: How should the phrase 'with loud instruments unto the LORD' be rendered?

sides.position: 'instruments of strength to Jehovah' — with which they ascribed power to God
'loud instruments,' as the Authorised Version, fitting the chronicler's taste

themes: the seven days of unleavened bread

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott: the Levites 'showed good skill for Jehovah' in their playing, and 'making confession' means yielding hearty thanks and acknowledging the Lord, not confessing sin.
Clarke calls teaching 'the good knowledge of God' the great work of every minister; Wesley reads their teaching office as the cause of the king's respect.
Henry reads the confession fully — religious, penitent, thankful, and supplicatory — and praises princes who encourage faithful preachers.
Gill: Hezekiah spoke 'to the heart' of the Levites, commending, exhorting, and promising protection.

debates.question: What is 'making confession' at the feast — thanksgiving, or the confession of sin?

sides.position: yielding thanks and acknowledging the Lord, not confessing guilt
a confession of several strands, including penitent confession of sin

schools.summary: Keil grounds the extra week in the abundance of thank-offerings (against Bertheau's reading), 'gave' meaning bestow as a heave-offering; Ellicott renders 'determined,' compares Solomon's double week (7:9), and marks the chronicler's love of festal joy.
Henry: so much comfort that they kept other seven days, inventing nothing new — 'the zeal of God's house made them forget their secular affairs' at harvest.
Gill: they consulted among themselves and with the king and nobles, and all agreed.

Keil records the sums, so abundant they sufficed for the added week, 'gave' being to set apart as a heave-offering; Ellicott renders 'had presented' (terumah) and marks the priests at last 'sanctified in multitude,' no longer hanging back as in 29:34.
Gill: Hezekiah gave from his own herds as heave offerings, for the people to feast on as thank-offerings.
Wesley weighs the generosity — given first to God, then to the people — as the more considerable at a reign's outset with an empty treasury, the surest proof of his piety.

Keil lays out three groups — Judah with its clergy, the congregation out of Israel, and the strangers from north and south, rejoicing without distinction; Ellicott fixes gerim as proselytes, distinct from garim (15:9), pointing to Lev. 17:12.
Gill sets the congregation of Judah first as the largest company, with its resident priests and Levites.
Clarke: the strangers were 'proselytes of the covenant,' circumcised Gentiles — none others could eat the Passover.
Keil and Ellicott match the feast only with Solomon's fourteen-day dedication (7:1) in length, richness, multitude, and joy; since Solomon all the tribes had never united at a feast.
Gill: the joy was not merely carnal but spiritual, from the restoration of the temple service.
Clarke: since Solomon the ten tribes had been separated, and now many joined to keep the Passover — the first reunion of north and south, a reversal of the schism.

Keil reads the ascended prayer as an inference from the blessing's fruit — later zeal (ch. 31) and rescue from Sennacherib (ch. 32); Ellicott confirms 'the Levitical priests,' the Aaronic blessing (Num. 6:23), and the omitted sacred Name.
Wesley: the blessing belonged to the Levites who were priests; Clarke turns to a mournful reflection on how soon the bright prospects were beclouded.
Gill: the priests who blessed were of the tribe of Levi, unlike the north's counterfeit priesthood; the Levites may have sung meanwhile.

outliers.note: Turns the blessing into an Arminian polemic on perseverance: those who draw back to perdition truly had saving grace, 'trifled with it, sinned against it,' and are therefore lost.

themes: the blessing proved by later mercies
